topics.title: Docker Basics
topics.summary: Package an app and its dependencies into an image and run it as an isolated container anywhere.
topics.description:
**Docker** packages your application together with its runtime, libraries and configuration into an **image**. A running instance of an image is a **container**. This removes the "works on my machine" problem.

### Key concepts
* **Image** - read-only template built from a `Dockerfile`, made of layers.
* **Container** - a running (isolated) process from an image.
* **Registry** - stores images (Docker Hub, GHCR, ECR).
* **Volume** - persistent storage outside the container's lifecycle.
* **Compose** - define several containers (app, DB, Redis) in one YAML file.

### Essential commands
* `docker build -t myapp .` - build an image.
* `docker run -p 3000:3000 myapp` - run and publish a port.
* `docker ps` / `docker logs <id>` / `docker exec -it <id> sh`.
* `docker stop <id>`, `docker rm <id>`, `docker images`.
* `docker compose up -d` - start the whole stack.

### Tips
* Use a small base image (`node:20-alpine`).
* Copy `package*.json` first and install, **then** copy the source - layer caching makes rebuilds fast.
* Add a `.dockerignore` (`node_modules`, `.git`).
* Never bake secrets into images; pass them as environment variables.
keyPoints: Dockerfile describes how to build an image
pitfalls: Storing data inside a container without a volume
Running as root and shipping secrets in the image
Copying the whole project before installing dependencies (breaks caching)

examples.title: Node.js Dockerfile
examples.code:
FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
examples.explanation: Dependency layer is cached until package.json changes.

examples.title: docker-compose.yml
examples.code:
services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports: ["3000:3000"]
    environment:
      - REDIS_URL=redis://redis:6379
    depends_on: [redis]
  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
examples.explanation: The API reaches Redis by its service name.

interview.a: An image is an immutable template; a container is a running instance created from it.
Containers share the host kernel and are lightweight and fast to start; VMs include a full guest OS.

topics.title: CI/CD Basics
topics.summary: Automatically build, test and deploy every change so releases become small, frequent and safe.
topics.description:
**CI (Continuous Integration)** - every push is automatically built and tested. **CD** means either *Continuous Delivery* (always releasable, deploy with one click) or *Continuous Deployment* (every passing change goes to production automatically).

### A typical pipeline
```
push / pull request
      |
      v
  install deps -> lint -> unit tests -> build
      |
      v
  build Docker image -> push to registry
      |
      v
  deploy to staging -> smoke tests
      |
      v
  deploy to production (manual approval or automatic)
```

### Benefits
* Bugs are caught minutes after they are written.
* Same repeatable process for every deploy.
* Small changes are easy to roll back.

### Good practices
* Keep the pipeline **fast** (cache dependencies, run jobs in parallel).
* Store secrets in the CI secret store, never in the repository.
* Protect `main`: require passing checks and review before merge.
* Deploy strategies: **rolling**, **blue-green**, **canary**; always have a **rollback** plan.
* Tools: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins, CircleCI.
keyPoints: CI = build and test on every change
Secrets live in the CI secret store
Plan rollbacks and use staged rollouts
pitfalls: Deploying straight from a developer laptop

examples.title: GitHub Actions workflow
examples.code:
name: CI
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 20, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm test
      - run: npm run build
examples.explanation: Runs on every push and pull request.

interview.a: Delivery keeps every build releasable but requires a manual approval to deploy; deployment ships every passing change automatically.
Releasing a new version to a small share of users first and watching metrics before rolling out fully.

topics.title: Android Emulator Stuck: Reset & Connect to Localhost
topics.summary: Commands to restart ADB, kill hung emulator processes on Windows, and how an emulator reaches your local API via 10.0.2.2.
topics.description:
When the Android emulator freezes, will not boot or `adb devices` shows nothing, the cure is to restart **ADB** (Android Debug Bridge) and kill leftover emulator processes.

### 1. Restart ADB
```
adb kill-server
adb start-server
adb devices
```

### 2. Kill a specific emulator
```
adb -s emulator-5554 emu kill
```

### 3. Kill hung processes on Windows
Find them first, then kill by PID:
```
tasklist | findstr emulator
tasklist | findstr qemu
taskkill /PID 17560 /F
```

**The shortcut that solves most cases** - kill by image name:
```
taskkill /IM emulator.exe /F
taskkill /IM qemu-system-x86_64.exe /F
```

### 4. Reaching your computer from the emulator
Inside the emulator `localhost` is the emulator itself. Your development machine is available at the special address **10.0.2.2**, so an API running on port 3000 is:
```
API_URL=http://10.0.2.2:3000/api/v1
```
Then start the app with `npm run android` (React Native).

For a **physical device** use your PC's LAN IP, or `adb reverse tcp:3000 tcp:3000` to forward the port.
keyPoints: Emulator reaches the host machine at 10.0.2.2
pitfalls: Using `localhost` in the API URL inside the emulator
Killing only emulator.exe and leaving qemu running
Forgetting to restart the Metro/app after changing `API_URL`

examples.title: Full recovery sequence (Windows)
examples.code:
taskkill /IM emulator.exe /F
taskkill /IM qemu-system-x86_64.exe /F
adb kill-server
adb start-server
adb devices
npm run android
examples.explanation: Kill processes, restart ADB, confirm device, run the app.

interview.q: What is 10.0.2.2 in the Android emulator?
interview.a: A special alias that points to the host computer's loopback interface (127.0.0.1 of your development machine).
